title: Use of Cholinesterase Inhibitors in People Living With HIV and HAND (HIV-Associated Neurocognitive Disorder): An Integrative Review
content: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) depletes CD4+ lymphocytes, compromising cellular immunity and increasing susceptibility to opportunistic infections. Additionally, HIV can lead to neurocognitive, motor, and sensory impairments known as HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND), which encompass symptoms ranging from concentration difficulties and psychomotor slowing to depressive states, irritability, and, in advanced stages, dementia. Cholinesterase inhibitors, commonly used in Alzheimer's disease, are a potential therapeutic option for cognitive decline in HAND. An integrative literature review was conducted using PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library databases to identify relevant studies on the use of cholinesterase inhibitors in individuals diagnosed with HAND. The literature search yielded studies that explore the efficacy and safety of cholinesterase inhibitors in HAND, highlighting both potential cognitive benefits and the need for further evidence. However, findings remain limited and inconclusive regarding robust clinical recommendations. While cholinesterase inhibitors represent a promising therapeutic approach for HAND-related cognitive decline, current evidence is insufficient to support widespread clinical use. Further controlled studies are necessary to establish their efficacy and safety in this specific population.
